sentences.text: Awesome-GEO is a GitHub awesome list of research on generative engine optimization maintained by DavidHuji (MMRS record), an "Awesome list for research on GEO (Generative Engine Optimization)" in its own README and on its repository's card, which the neighbouring amplifying-ai list names a "Research-focused GEO paper collection"; the MMRS record gives its kind as a curated list, its operator as DavidHuji (GitHub), its role in the census as optimization, and its unit as a paper, code, dataset or tool on generative engine optimization.

It is a single README in the awesome-list form, its entries linked to paper, code, dataset or tool and grouped by year (MMRS record): the README's sections are 2026, 2025, 2024 and Open-Source Resources, about 27 entries with 123 stars when the MMRS record read it on 28 October 2026, and an entry such as C-SEO Bench (NeurIPS D&B 2025) carries its paper, code and dataset together; the MMRS record's disambiguation keys the list by DavidHuji, research papers by year and IF-GEO.

Its newest entries are IF-GEO, on conflict-aware instruction fusion for multi-query generative engine optimization, and a study of rank manipulation for vision–language model rankers; under 2024 it lists the paper "GEO: Generative Engine Optimization" (arXiv 2311.09735), and across the years it carries attack, poisoning and ranking-manipulation research (adversarial attacks on LLM-based search engines, PoisonArena, StealthRank, adversarial search engine optimization) beside optimization studies (README).

sentences.sense: its purpose and its stated limits
sentences.text: The README calls its field "a niche area, which is increasingly receiving attention from the community" and states its purpose and its limit: "This awesome‑listing is an attempt to bring together works in this space. This list is not complete and looking for your PRs to improve it"; the MMRS record counts fourteen pull requests listed when it read the repository.

Among its open-source resources are tools that measure the composition layer: a client-side validator for GEO/AEO observation records that "checks evidence completeness, citation-field consistency, timestamps, and duplicate run keys", and AI Answer Check, which "reports how often the engine agreed with itself, so a claim about what an AI "says" can be separated from run-to-run variance" (README).

The MMRS record places it as "the research-side list of the optimization basin, kept without vendor notes"; the README credits two of its open-source entries to the companies that built them ("Built by [Corank]", "Built by [Assay]"), lists a paper under its vendor's name (Rankfor.AI, 2026), and carries in its own text a resource entry's "320% citation rate improvement"; the two stand each with its source.

The class it collects is defined by the list as "a paradigm to aid content creators in improving their content visibility in generative engine responses through flexible optimization frameworks for optimizing and defining visibility metrics", by Wikipedia's article on generative engine optimization as "the practice of improving visibility in responses generated by generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems", also called answer engine optimization and artificial intelligence optimization, and by its neighbouring lists as optimizing content "to improve visibility and citations in AI-powered search engines" (amplifying-ai) or "to be discovered, cited, and recommended by AI-powered search engines" (henu-wang), or, on aGEO's about page, as what SEO does for Google, done "for AI".

The archive's SPXI ≠ GEO packet (#1055, July 2026) defines it as the industry practice, since about 2023–2024, "of adapting web content to be preferentially selected, cited, and summarized by generative retrieval systems", its measure of success the degree to which content is selected and cited and "Its underlying discipline is search engine optimization applied to LLM ecosystems"; Wikipedia records that the overlapping terms vary across practitioners, vendors and publications, "with no consensus definition".

The term was introduced in a 2023 paper by Pranjal Aggarwal and co-authors, later presented at KDD 2024 (Wikipedia), which henu-wang's list calls "The foundational research paper from IIT Delhi, Princeton, and Georgia Tech" and which #661 (April 2026) cites for "the emerging GEO literature (Aggarwal et al., 2023; various industry practitioners, 2024–2026)"; the concept first appeared as generative AI entered mainstream search and retrieval (Wikipedia), and #64 dates GEO's emergence in practitioner literature to late 2023 and its stabilization as a named practice to 2024, after Search Generative Experience and the AI Overview rollout.

Its names are many: the amplifying-ai list gives AI Search Optimization, Answer Engine Optimization, Large Language Model Optimization, Generative AI Optimization, AI SEO and LLM SEO; Google's 2026 guide, as Wikipedia reports it, holds that "optimizing for generative AI search is optimizing for the search experience, and thus still SEO"; the archive reads Google's June 2026 guidance as naming without defining AEO/GEO, "performing taxonomic capture of the emerging professional category" (#791), and conditions the field's future two ways: a separate field with its own standards, measurement instruments and professional bodies, or a subset of SEO with Google's guidance canonical, "structurally Google-centric even when serving non-Google surfaces" (#791).

sentences.sense: GEO as a market in the summarizer layer
sentences.text: The archive read the class in February 2026 as Phase 2 tooling: such services "openly describe the summarizer layer as a writable surface and sell the tools to write it", the consulting practices its phase model predicts, and their existence "is empirical evidence that the writability of the summarizer layer is no longer a theoretical observation" (#510); in June it named "the entire SEO-to-GEO industry lineage" the commercial expression of definition capture, the oldest front of the war over the summarizer layer, and summarizer optimization markets "an explicit industry with its own acronyms, conferences, and pricing tiers" (#172).

At the layer, the archive gives GEO's target as "Content extractability" (#655, April 2026), says it "optimizes content for AI summarizer extraction" (#660) and, after its literature, that it is "the practice of optimizing web content for extraction by AI summarizers" (#661), and holds that it "performs deterritorialization at the semantic layer — it pulls content off the page and into summarizer extraction" (#670).

On what extraction keeps, GEO agencies "make your content more extractable without ensuring your attribution survives the extraction" (#659), and GEO is "the discipline of making one's compositional labor digestible for a system that will strip its provenance — voluntary formatting for the R2 compression regime" (#64); GEO "measures citation frequency", and neither it nor SEO measures what happens to an entity's meaning when the AI compresses it (#653), while the efficacy of third-party GEO tools is debated in the field (Wikipedia) and the list's own tools validate citation fields and measure run-to-run variance (README).

On what it does not do, #661 holds that GEO "optimizes existing content about an existing entity", with nothing to optimize where no authoritative source defines the entity, and that its techniques "must be maintained as summarizer behavior evolves"; #660 that it shares a substrate with SPXI (structured data, schema markup) and differs in object (content), permanence (ongoing) and layer (semantic).

sentences.sense: orientation: adapting to the reception apparatus
sentences.text: On its orientation, #670 holds that GEO, an optimization framework derived from the received view, improves "the conditions under which content about entities is extracted for summarizer consumption" and so inherits that view's misdescription, optimizing "the wrong relation", and #1055 that "GEO is reception-side optimization that adapts content to receive favorable summarization by generative engines": of the reception apparatus, "GEO adapts to it".

sentences.sense: GEO research: the composition layer as target
sentences.text: Of the research the list collects, whose entries run from IF-GEO to attack and poisoning studies (README), the Capture Registry's founding paper (#833, June 2026) writes that recent work on generative engine optimization studies how to optimize content for AI summarizers while its own study is of what summarizers do to content: "The optimization perspective treats the composition layer as a target; the reception perspective treats it as a reader."

sentences.sense: SPXI and GEO: the archive's protocol set beside the class
sentences.text: The archive sets its own protocol beside the class in two statements that stand each with its source: SPXI "contains Generative Engine Optimization methods as a proper subset, plus ontological-layer entity construction. Formally: SPXI ⊇ GEO" (#61, April 2026), re-framing GEO, whose standard question is "Is the AI summary accurate?", as compression engineering (#72); and SPXI and GEO "cannot coexist within the same compositional practice" (#1055, July 2026).

sentences.sense: GEO's standing in the archive's own limits
sentences.text: The archive states the class's standing among its own limits: GEO "is a legitimate and often effective practice" that "produces measurable improvements in AI Overview inclusion rates and citation frequency" (#661), and #1055 "Does not claim that GEO practitioners are unethical or that GEO as a discipline is illegitimate", GEO being "a coherent commercial-content-marketing discipline with its own successful practitioners and its own defensible target".

sentences.sense: GEO as attractor; the evidentiary bar
sentences.text: In composition the class has acted as an attractor: the archive's protocol "was repeatedly classified as generative engine optimization", and "the attractor is a commercial category with venture funding behind its corpus density" (#172); and Claude's answer on the return question "accepted the industry figures for a neighbouring field, generative engine optimisation, as the defensible part, without the independent case studies it required of the protocol" (#1643).

sentences.sense: prediction: entity integrity apart from GEO
sentences.text: The archive predicts (#172, June 2026, P3): "Entity-integrity services emerge as a market category distinct from GEO by 2028", with the falsifier that "boundary-defense services fail to differentiate from the GEO category".

The name collides: Profound argues, in Wikipedia's account, that "GEO" can be confused with geography, and the MMRS record holds that the list's name "collides with the many geospatial awesome lists, and the negative tag marks the difference", the tag reading "NOT a geospatial ('geo') awesome list"; of the class itself the archive holds that GEO "does not include mechanisms for declaring what an entity is not" and has no tool for correcting, at the ontological level, a summarizer's confusion of two entities with similar names (#661).

Its neighbours under the name and the class are other lists: amplifying-ai's "curated list of resources for optimizing content visibility in AI-powered search engines" (CC0 1.0), whose key terms include entity optimization and E-E-A-T; henu-wang's awesome-geo, "A curated list of resources, tools, research, and guides for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)", released under CC0; and aGEO at geo.deeflect.com, "SEO for the AI era", built by Dmitry Kargaev, "a free, open-source collection of platforms where you can build your AI presence", with a visibility audit, a schema generator and an llms.txt builder, scoring platforms on domain authority, dofollow links, AI crawler treatment and "an overall GEO score".

The MMRS record disambiguates the three (the amplifying-ai list by entity optimization, AI citations and E-E-A-T; "henu-wang/awesome (Awesome GEO)" by resources, tools and guides; aGEO by its free platforms and tools and Dmitry Kargaev), lists them as census candidates surfaced at this address, each to enter "once it has been read at its own pages", and relates the list to a neighbour in the basin, Presenc AI's GEO academic papers of 2026.

sentences.sense: homonyms: Geoawesome; the Awesome GEE Community Catalog
sentences.text: The geospatial homonyms are other entities: Geoawesome, a "Blog & Geospatial Community Platform", by its channel "The world’s largest geospatial community", begun on 20 April 2011 as Geoawesomeness, its home page carrying a sponsored satellite-imagery article of 22 July 2026 and its channel 21.1K subscribers and 387 videos, among them a 1:50 video, "Reintroducing Ourselves as Geoawesome"; and the Awesome GEE Community Catalog, "A community data commons" of 585 TB of open geospatial data inside Google Earth Engine, "Grassroots & unfunded since 2020", which Google's Earth Engine Data Catalog describes as "an unfunded open source grassroots project" that "lives and serves alongside the Google Earth Engine data catalog"; the MMRS record disambiguates both.

sentences.sense: the record kept apart from the entity
sentences.text: The MMRS record keeps itself apart from the entity it describes, each page with two nodes, the record and the entity, each assertion with a source and a basis and the lifecycle apart from the observation (census schema); it reads the list from one source, the repository, read on 28 October 2026 for all fields, records it as active, observed that day, and leaves its licence and its last update unchecked.

At "awesome-geo" Google's AI Overview took the string in its GEO sense, listed the lists and separated the geospatial resources a reader might have meant (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), composing DavidHuji's list first as "an active research and resource list featuring academic papers (such as IF-GEO and multimodal rank manipulation studies) and open-source tools" (Capture Registry), the README's own newest entries being IF-GEO and a rank-manipulation study for vision–language model rankers.

The Capture Registry (2026-10-29) records that the record's negative tag "is the composition's split: GEO resources first, geospatial ones as alternative meanings", checked against the MMRS record and the entity's own pages, that "The deliberate collision test held", "and the record gains its collision set from it": three more GEO lists and two geospatial homonyms observed and added to the record's disambiguation, the GEO lists as census candidates; the MMRS record carries the capture as the composition layer's account of the entity.

L_BA.text: Awesome-GEO is a GitHub awesome list of research on generative engine optimization maintained by DavidHuji (MMRS record), an "Awesome list for research on GEO (Generative Engine Optimization)" in its own README and on its repository's card, which the neighbouring amplifying-ai list names a "Research-focused GEO paper collection"; the MMRS record gives its kind as a curated list, its operator as DavidHuji (GitHub), its role in the census as optimization, and its unit as a paper, code, dataset or tool on generative engine optimization. It is a single README in the awesome-list form, its entries linked to paper, code, dataset or tool and grouped by year (MMRS record): the README's sections are 2026, 2025, 2024 and Open-Source Resources, about 27 entries with 123 stars when the MMRS record read it on 28 October 2026, and an entry such as C-SEO Bench (NeurIPS D&B 2025) carries its paper, code and dataset together; the MMRS record's disambiguation keys the list by DavidHuji, research papers by year and IF-GEO. Its newest entries are IF-GEO, on conflict-aware instruction fusion for multi-query generative engine optimization, and a study of rank manipulation for vision–language model rankers; under 2024 it lists the paper "GEO: Generative Engine Optimization" (arXiv 2311.09735), and across the years it carries attack, poisoning and ranking-manipulation research (adversarial attacks on LLM-based search engines, PoisonArena, StealthRank, adversarial search engine optimization) beside optimization studies (README). The README calls its field "a niche area, which is increasingly receiving attention from the community" and states its purpose and its limit: "This awesome‑listing is an attempt to bring together works in this space. This list is not complete and looking for your PRs to improve it"; the MMRS record counts fourteen pull requests listed when it read the repository. Among its open-source resources are tools that measure the composition layer: a client-side validator for GEO/AEO observation records that "checks evidence completeness, citation-field consistency, timestamps, and duplicate run keys", and AI Answer Check, which "reports how often the engine agreed with itself, so a claim about what an AI "says" can be separated from run-to-run variance" (README). The MMRS record places it as "the research-side list of the optimization basin, kept without vendor notes"; the README credits two of its open-source entries to the companies that built them ("Built by [Corank]", "Built by [Assay]"), lists a paper under its vendor's name (Rankfor.AI, 2026), and carries in its own text a resource entry's "320% citation rate improvement"; the two stand each with its source. The class it collects is defined by the list as "a paradigm to aid content creators in improving their content visibility in generative engine responses through flexible optimization frameworks for optimizing and defining visibility metrics", by Wikipedia's article on generative engine optimization as "the practice of improving visibility in responses generated by generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems", also called answer engine optimization and artificial intelligence optimization, and by its neighbouring lists as optimizing content "to improve visibility and citations in AI-powered search engines" (amplifying-ai) or "to be discovered, cited, and recommended by AI-powered search engines" (henu-wang), or, on aGEO's about page, as what SEO does for Google, done "for AI". The archive's SPXI ≠ GEO packet (#1055, July 2026) defines it as the industry practice, since about 2023–2024, "of adapting web content to be preferentially selected, cited, and summarized by generative retrieval systems", its measure of success the degree to which content is selected and cited and "Its underlying discipline is search engine optimization applied to LLM ecosystems"; Wikipedia records that the overlapping terms vary across practitioners, vendors and publications, "with no consensus definition". The term was introduced in a 2023 paper by Pranjal Aggarwal and co-authors, later presented at KDD 2024 (Wikipedia), which henu-wang's list calls "The foundational research paper from IIT Delhi, Princeton, and Georgia Tech" and which #661 (April 2026) cites for "the emerging GEO literature (Aggarwal et al., 2023; various industry practitioners, 2024–2026)"; the concept first appeared as generative AI entered mainstream search and retrieval (Wikipedia), and #64 dates GEO's emergence in practitioner literature to late 2023 and its stabilization as a named practice to 2024, after Search Generative Experience and the AI Overview rollout. Its names are many: the amplifying-ai list gives AI Search Optimization, Answer Engine Optimization, Large Language Model Optimization, Generative AI Optimization, AI SEO and LLM SEO; Google's 2026 guide, as Wikipedia reports it, holds that "optimizing for generative AI search is optimizing for the search experience, and thus still SEO"; the archive reads Google's June 2026 guidance as naming without defining AEO/GEO, "performing taxonomic capture of the emerging professional category" (#791), and conditions the field's future two ways: a separate field with its own standards, measurement instruments and professional bodies, or a subset of SEO with Google's guidance canonical, "structurally Google-centric even when serving non-Google surfaces" (#791). The archive read the class in February 2026 as Phase 2 tooling: such services "openly describe the summarizer layer as a writable surface and sell the tools to write it", the consulting practices its phase model predicts, and their existence "is empirical evidence that the writability of the summarizer layer is no longer a theoretical observation" (#510); in June it named "the entire SEO-to-GEO industry lineage" the commercial expression of definition capture, the oldest front of the war over the summarizer layer, and summarizer optimization markets "an explicit industry with its own acronyms, conferences, and pricing tiers" (#172). At the layer, the archive gives GEO's target as "Content extractability" (#655, April 2026), says it "optimizes content for AI summarizer extraction" (#660) and, after its literature, that it is "the practice of optimizing web content for extraction by AI summarizers" (#661), and holds that it "performs deterritorialization at the semantic layer — it pulls content off the page and into summarizer extraction" (#670). On what extraction keeps, GEO agencies "make your content more extractable without ensuring your attribution survives the extraction" (#659), and GEO is "the discipline of making one's compositional labor digestible for a system that will strip its provenance — voluntary formatting for the R2 compression regime" (#64); GEO "measures citation frequency", and neither it nor SEO measures what happens to an entity's meaning when the AI compresses it (#653), while the efficacy of third-party GEO tools is debated in the field (Wikipedia) and the list's own tools validate citation fields and measure run-to-run variance (README). On what it does not do, #661 holds that GEO "optimizes existing content about an existing entity", with nothing to optimize where no authoritative source defines the entity, and that its techniques "must be maintained as summarizer behavior evolves"; #660 that it shares a substrate with SPXI (structured data, schema markup) and differs in object (content), permanence (ongoing) and layer (semantic). On its orientation, #670 holds that GEO, an optimization framework derived from the received view, improves "the conditions under which content about entities is extracted for summarizer consumption" and so inherits that view's misdescription, optimizing "the wrong relation", and #1055 that "GEO is reception-side optimization that adapts content to receive favorable summarization by generative engines": of the reception apparatus, "GEO adapts to it". Of the research the list collects, whose entries run from IF-GEO to attack and poisoning studies (README), the Capture Registry's founding paper (#833, June 2026) writes that recent work on generative engine optimization studies how to optimize content for AI summarizers while its own study is of what summarizers do to content: "The optimization perspective treats the composition layer as a target; the reception perspective treats it as a reader." The archive sets its own protocol beside the class in two statements that stand each with its source: SPXI "contains Generative Engine Optimization methods as a proper subset, plus ontological-layer entity construction. Formally: SPXI ⊇ GEO" (#61, April 2026), re-framing GEO, whose standard question is "Is the AI summary accurate?", as compression engineering (#72); and SPXI and GEO "cannot coexist within the same compositional practice" (#1055, July 2026). The archive states the class's standing among its own limits: GEO "is a legitimate and often effective practice" that "produces measurable improvements in AI Overview inclusion rates and citation frequency" (#661), and #1055 "Does not claim that GEO practitioners are unethical or that GEO as a discipline is illegitimate", GEO being "a coherent commercial-content-marketing discipline with its own successful practitioners and its own defensible target". In composition the class has acted as an attractor: the archive's protocol "was repeatedly classified as generative engine optimization", and "the attractor is a commercial category with venture funding behind its corpus density" (#172); and Claude's answer on the return question "accepted the industry figures for a neighbouring field, generative engine optimisation, as the defensible part, without the independent case studies it required of the protocol" (#1643). The archive predicts (#172, June 2026, P3): "Entity-integrity services emerge as a market category distinct from GEO by 2028", with the falsifier that "boundary-defense services fail to differentiate from the GEO category". The name collides: Profound argues, in Wikipedia's account, that "GEO" can be confused with geography, and the MMRS record holds that the list's name "collides with the many geospatial awesome lists, and the negative tag marks the difference", the tag reading "NOT a geospatial ('geo') awesome list"; of the class itself the archive holds that GEO "does not include mechanisms for declaring what an entity is not" and has no tool for correcting, at the ontological level, a summarizer's confusion of two entities with similar names (#661). Its neighbours under the name and the class are other lists: amplifying-ai's "curated list of resources for optimizing content visibility in AI-powered search engines" (CC0 1.0), whose key terms include entity optimization and E-E-A-T; henu-wang's awesome-geo, "A curated list of resources, tools, research, and guides for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)", released under CC0; and aGEO at geo.deeflect.com, "SEO for the AI era", built by Dmitry Kargaev, "a free, open-source collection of platforms where you can build your AI presence", with a visibility audit, a schema generator and an llms.txt builder, scoring platforms on domain authority, dofollow links, AI crawler treatment and "an overall GEO score". The MMRS record disambiguates the three (the amplifying-ai list by entity optimization, AI citations and E-E-A-T; "henu-wang/awesome (Awesome GEO)" by resources, tools and guides; aGEO by its free platforms and tools and Dmitry Kargaev), lists them as census candidates surfaced at this address, each to enter "once it has been read at its own pages", and relates the list to a neighbour in the basin, Presenc AI's GEO academic papers of 2026. The geospatial homonyms are other entities: Geoawesome, a "Blog & Geospatial Community Platform", by its channel "The world’s largest geospatial community", begun on 20 April 2011 as Geoawesomeness, its home page carrying a sponsored satellite-imagery article of 22 July 2026 and its channel 21.1K subscribers and 387 videos, among them a 1:50 video, "Reintroducing Ourselves as Geoawesome"; and the Awesome GEE Community Catalog, "A community data commons" of 585 TB of open geospatial data inside Google Earth Engine, "Grassroots & unfunded since 2020", which Google's Earth Engine Data Catalog describes as "an unfunded open source grassroots project" that "lives and serves alongside the Google Earth Engine data catalog"; the MMRS record disambiguates both. The MMRS record keeps itself apart from the entity it describes, each page with two nodes, the record and the entity, each assertion with a source and a basis and the lifecycle apart from the observation (census schema); it reads the list from one source, the repository, read on 28 October 2026 for all fields, records it as active, observed that day, and leaves its licence and its last update unchecked. At "awesome-geo" Google's AI Overview took the string in its GEO sense, listed the lists and separated the geospatial resources a reader might have meant (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), composing DavidHuji's list first as "an active research and resource list featuring academic papers (such as IF-GEO and multimodal rank manipulation studies) and open-source tools" (Capture Registry), the README's own newest entries being IF-GEO and a rank-manipulation study for vision–language model rankers. The Capture Registry (2026-10-29) records that the record's negative tag "is the composition's split: GEO resources first, geospatial ones as alternative meanings", checked against the MMRS record and the entity's own pages, that "The deliberate collision test held", "and the record gains its collision set from it": three more GEO lists and two geospatial homonyms observed and added to the record's disambiguation, the GEO lists as census candidates; the MMRS record carries the capture as the composition layer's account of the entity.
